extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media professionals, media critics and press-watchers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality and practices of news reporting with respect to originality, fact-checking, sources, staffing and the influence of PR/wire copy. Focuses on routine day-to-day journalism rather than only investigative pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our job as journalists is to tell the truth, but repeatedly we fail." (authoritative statement of journalism's core duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth-telling is the central obligation of journalism; evaluate stories against whether they genuinely pursue and present accurate information rather than echoing misleading or false claims (examples cited: WMDs, millennium bugs, routine disinformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid churnalism / passive processing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where once we were active gatherers of news, we have become passive processors of second-hand material generated by the booming PR industry and a handful of wire agencies... The relentless impact of commercialisation has seen our journalism reduced to mere churnalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject simply reprinting or lightly editing press releases and agency copy. Reporters should actively generate reporting—making contacts, pursuing leads and independently verifying claims—rather than mass-producing copy from incoming material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend sufficient time out reporting and building contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Case example: a provincial reporter turned out 48 stories in a week but spent only three hours out of the office and spoke face to face to only four people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporters' workloads and time allocation: reporters producing very high volumes with minimal time spent interviewing or in the field cannot be expected to develop leads, check facts or produce reliable journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original reporter-generated content (traceable provenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiff research: only 12% of examined stories were provably based on material generated by Fleet Street reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer and reward stories demonstrably produced from reporters' own reporting. When evaluating a story, trace its origin (reporter notes, interviews) to confirm whether it is original reporting or derived from PR/agency material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and disclose PR input
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiff finding: 54% of stories contained clear signs of PR input (conservative estimate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and minimise PR-origin material in news pages. Recognise that PR is often designed to serve commercial or political interests; verify PR-supplied claims independently and be transparent about reliance on PR sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on agency (wire) copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiff finding: 70% of quality news stories were wholly or partly recycled from agency copy (usually the Press Association).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat agency copy as a source to be supplemented and checked, not a substitute for reporter-generated reporting. Overreliance reduces distinctiveness and independent verification in newsroom output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughly fact-check central statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardiff researchers found that only 12% of stories which relied on a specific statement of fact showed evidence that the central statement had been thoroughly checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require documented fact-checking for any central factual claim in a story. Evidence of checking (corroborating sources, documents, on-the-record confirmations) should be present for key assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine practice of news judgement, balance and source interrogation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted conclusion: everyday practices of "news judgement, fact-checking, balance, criticising and interrogating sources" are central to routine journalism but are becoming exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether journalists apply independent news judgement, seek balance, critically interrogate sources and challenge narratives as part of standard daily practice, not only in investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match staffing to editorial output and time requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Over 20 years editorial space trebled while average staffing levels are slightly lower; average time to find and check stories cut to a third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial staffing relative to the volume of editorial space and output. Insufficient staffing/time inevitably reduces reporting quality—hiring and workflow must allow time for sourcing and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability and transparency of story origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology: researchers attempted to capture all incoming material passed to reporters and tracked backwards to find source material; where in doubt they interviewed reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain records and transparency about the origin of information used in stories. When evaluating work, check source chains and be prepared to interview reporters to resolve origin questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist manipulation by intelligence agencies and political actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: "skilful manipulation of reporters by intelligence agencies and Downing Street in the run-up to the invasion of Iraq."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant for possible manipulation or seeded narratives from governmental or intelligence sources; independently verify such claims and treat official briefings with healthy scepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish investigative work from routine reporting but insist on basic standards for both
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes he is not only addressing investigative journalism but the everyday practices central to routine day-to-day journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While investigative pieces require deeper resources, routine reporting also must meet standards of checking, balance and source interrogation. Evaluate both kinds of work against appropriate, consistent baseline practices.
